profiles.meeting_scenario: At a military teaching hospital, the Surgical ICU (SICU) and anesthesia department are holding a coordination meeting midway through a 7-week rollout of a standardized preoperative SBAR handoff for SICU patients going to the OR. The immediate context is that both teams have completed initial training, but they now need to align on how the SBAR handoff will be used during weekday add-on cases and next-morning scheduled surgeries, how completion will be documented, and how progress will be reported to the evidence-based practice (EBP) lead before the end of week 4. The agenda is to confirm the handoff workflow between SICU and anesthesia, clarify who updates the shared tracking sheet and where documentation lives in the EHR, and agree on what counts as a completed SBAR for weekly implementation reporting. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear division of responsibilities and a shared plan for the next two weeks of implementation monitoring.

members.name: Maj. Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Critical care nursing workflow, staff education, handoff standardization, quality-improvement reporting
members.background: A senior Army nurse who has spent eight years in adult critical care and now oversees practice-change rollouts in the SICU; she helped adapt the SBAR form for bedside nurses and has been collecting unit-level implementation data for the project team.
members.private_state: She wants the SICU nurses to experience the rollout as lightweight and sustainable, and she is worried that if documentation feels duplicative or too rigid, bedside adoption will drop and the project will lose momentum.
hidden_assumptions: When the project team asks whether an 'SBAR was completed,' it means the SICU nurse used the standardized SBAR form and entered the key fields in the designated nursing handoff section before transport.

The 'anesthesia handoff' refers to the direct nurse-to-anesthesia exchange that happens once the receiving anesthesia clinician is assigned and available, typically near physical transfer out of the SICU.
The shared implementation tracker is a nursing-owned quality tool, so anesthesia will confirm completion informally but SICU is the team that updates the official weekly counts.
For scheduled first-case surgeries, preparing the SBAR during the night shift counts as having the patient 'ready for surgery' as long as the note is current when transport is called.

members.name: Lt. Col. Daniel Harper
members.role: Chief CRNA and Anesthesia Operations Lead
members.expertise: Perioperative anesthesia workflow, pre-op readiness, OR scheduling coordination, cross-unit process implementation
members.background: A career military CRNA who supervises daily anesthesia staffing and coordinates communication between anesthesia providers, the OR desk, and ICU teams for critically ill surgical patients.
members.private_state: He wants a reliable process that gives anesthesia actionable patient information early enough to allocate staff and prevent day-of-surgery surprises, and he is concerned that nurses may wait too long to communicate changes.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says an 'SBAR was completed,' it includes a live verbal handoff to the anesthesia provider who will cover the case, not just documentation in the chart.
The 'anesthesia handoff' begins as soon as the OR schedule indicates a likely case and can be given to the board runner or assigned CRNA the evening before or early that morning.

Because anesthesia needs the data for operational planning, the shared tracker should be updated by whichever anesthesia lead receives the handoff, since they can verify that the exchange actually happened.
A patient is only 'ready for surgery' for handoff purposes once the latest airway, vasoactive infusion, and antibiotic status have been verbally reconfirmed on the day of surgery.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to report the number of patients with a 'completed SBAR' each week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes completion means the SICU nurse filled out the standardized SBAR tool in the nursing workflow and documented it in the intended EHR section before transfer.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes completion means the standardized content was actually delivered verbally to an anesthesia clinician in real time, with enough exchange to support anesthesia preparation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In implementation meetings, 'completed SBAR' sounds like an established project metric, so each assumes the other is using the familiar common-sense definition tied to their own workflow; both also view documentation and verbal exchange as naturally coupled, so the difference remains invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: Which anesthesia contact the handoff is for
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss giving the handoff 'to anesthesia' before the patient goes to the OR.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the anesthesia clinician definitively taking the patient, usually the assigned CRNA or anesthesiologist available around transport time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of whichever anesthesia operations person is managing the case earliest, such as the board runner, charge CRNA, or preliminary assignee, even if the final in-room provider changes later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In day-to-day hospital speech, 'anesthesia' is routinely used as a collective destination rather than a specific person, so both participants hear the phrase as entirely normal and do not notice they are anchoring it to different recipients.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'we'll update the tracker' so the EBP lead has current numbers every Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes SICU charge nurses or the educator will update the shared spreadsheet from nursing documentation and only reach out if a handoff seems unclear.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the anesthesia lead who received the handoff will mark the tracker, because receipt is the only reliable proof that the workflow occurred as intended.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The tracker is discussed as a routine administrative artifact rather than a contested workflow step, and both parties assume the obvious owner is the team already using it in their own local process.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to patients who are 'ready for surgery tomorrow' when deciding when the SBAR should happen.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients posted for next-day surgery with the current plan stable enough that the night nurse can prepare the SBAR in advance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patients whose same-day operative readiness has been reconfirmed that morning, including current lines, drips, and antibiotic timing, making them actionable for anesthesia planning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operationally obvious and both use it fluently in perioperative contexts, but each role has a different habitual threshold for readiness; because both thresholds are reasonable, neither hears the wording as ambiguous.

turns.inner_thought: We are at the point where this either feels routine for the bedside nurses or it starts to feel like one more burdensome project. I need today's discussion to lock in a simple flow: SICU nurses use the standardized SBAR form, document it in the nursing handoff section before transport, and then I can keep pulling the weekly numbers without adding extra steps. If we keep the expectations lightweight, adoption will hold through week 4.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Since we're moving into week 4 of the rollout, I wanted to make sure we're aligned on the handoff flow, where the documentation should live, and how we'll handle Friday reporting on the pre-op SBARs.

turns.inner_thought: The process is improving, but the real value is only there if anesthesia hears about these patients early enough to plan coverage and catch problems before the OR day gets chaotic. When I say tomorrow's cases, I mean patients whose status has been reconfirmed and is actionable for the morning. And 'to anesthesia' can be the board runner or charge CRNA as soon as the schedule starts taking shape; it doesn't have to wait for the final in-room provider.
turns.utterance: From our side, we're already seeing better consistency. What I want to preserve is making sure anesthesia gets the handoff early enough for tomorrow's cases and for the same-day add-ons, so we're not trying to sort things out at the last minute.

turns.inner_thought: For the SICU, if a patient is posted for first case and the plan is stable overnight, the night nurse can complete the standardized SBAR form in the chart and that should count. Then the day shift isn't scrambling, and we avoid duplicate work. As long as the note is current when transport is called, that patient is ready for surgery tomorrow in my mind.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For patients who are ready for surgery tomorrow, the night nurse can usually complete the SBAR and have it available before transport is even arranged, which has helped smooth things out on our end.

turns.inner_thought: That timing is fine if the information actually reaches anesthesia early enough to affect staffing and preparation. A completed SBAR to me means the content has been delivered in a live exchange, not just sitting in the chart. If we have it before the patient rolls, we can decide whether we need a different skill mix, prep for airway issues, or troubleshoot antibiotics and drips.
turns.utterance: That should work well, as long as anesthesia has the SBAR early. We use that information to line up staffing and flag issues before the patient rolls down.

turns.inner_thought: Our nurses have generally been waiting until the receiving anesthesia clinician is actually identified and available near transfer, because that's when the exchange is most relevant and least likely to create duplicate calls. I want to make sure that timing hasn't been frustrating for them, but I don't want to commit the unit to chasing multiple anesthesia contacts for every case.
turns.utterance: What we've been doing is having the nurse hand off to anesthesia once the receiving provider is identified. Has that timing been adequate from your side?

turns.inner_thought: Adequate, yes, as long as 'to anesthesia' means it reaches whichever operational anesthesia lead is managing the case when the board is being built. It can come to the charge CRNA or board runner first; I don't need it to wait for the final assignment. If they keep treating anesthesia as a collective destination, this should be easy enough to absorb.
turns.utterance: Yes, as long as the information reaches anesthesia when the board is being finalized. Even if it goes first through the charge CRNA or board runner, that still helps us a lot.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can keep the reporting process anchored in nursing documentation. I already know where the standardized form lives in the EHR, and I can pull the count of completed SBARs from that section for the EBP lead. The tracker has really been a nursing quality tool up to this point, so I expect SICU will remain the source of the official weekly numbers.
turns.utterance: Perfect. On the reporting piece, I was planning to send the EBP lead the weekly count of completed SBARs, and I can pull those numbers from the nursing handoff documentation.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me if the tracker reflects actual receipt by anesthesia, because that's the only way I know the exchange truly happened. Ideally, whichever anesthesia lead gets the handoff should update the shared sheet in real time. Then Friday's numbers will be cleaner and won't overstate completion based on charting alone.
turns.utterance: I think that fits. If we update the tracker when anesthesia receives the handoff, that should keep the Friday numbers clean and make sure the count reflects what actually came through.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me—he's probably just saying anesthesia can help verify informally. My charge nurses are already reviewing whether the SBAR form was completed each morning for SICU patients headed to the OR, so the workflow doesn't need to change. We'll keep owning the spreadsheet and reach out if something seems unclear.
turns.utterance: That's fine. Our charge nurses are already reviewing the form completion each morning for patients headed to the OR, so we should be able to keep the tracker current without much trouble.

turns.inner_thought: For first starts, I need day-of-surgery confirmation of the current airway picture, active drips, and antibiotic timing. A completed SBAR isn't really actionable until those points are verbally reconfirmed that morning. If they treat tomorrow's cases as settled overnight, we may still get surprised unless the morning exchange happens.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd emphasize for first-start cases: I especially want the antibiotic plan, airway concerns, and current drips confirmed in the SBAR on the day of surgery.

turns.inner_thought: Those fields are already built into the standardized tool, so I don't want the nurses thinking they need to recreate the whole handoff again in the morning unless something has changed. For patients ready for surgery tomorrow, the night-shift SBAR should stand as long as the clinical picture stays the same. That keeps the process sustainable.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. Those items are already in the tool, and the nurses will keep using the same SBAR for tomorrow's surgical patients unless something changes overnight.

turns.inner_thought: Great—then anesthesia can expect those handoffs to come through early, and my leads can mark the tracker when they receive them. I'll assume we're set on anesthesia keeping that part current and that we'll see next week whether the weekday add-ons and first cases are settling into a reliable pattern.
turns.utterance: Great. Then anesthesia will watch for those handoffs, we'll keep the tracker current, and we'll touch base next week on how the process is going.
